academic achievement is a function of neuropsychological status and the severity of the child's behavioral disturbance.

the relationship between the severity of psychiatric disorders, neuropsychological factors and academic achievement.

the neuropsychological factors are most important to consider in the assessment and treatment of children with significant psychiatric disorders.
the academic achievement of children with psychiatric disorders is best predicted by the neuropsychological status and severity of their psychiatric disturbance.

children with significant emotional disturbance and mental illness are more likely than their peers to have academic difficulties and that these difficulties can be predicted by neuropsychological factors more so than by demographic factors or IQ.

children with psychiatric disorders are not simply "slow" learners, but rather that they have a unique set of learning problems that are often not addressed by standard remedial programs.
